articles.title: Northrop Grumman Exec at AUSA on Biggest Defense Threats Facing Global Forces
articles.summary:
In this NYSE Live interview from the AUSA Annual Meeting & Exposition, JD Durkin speaks with Kenneth Padorov of Northrop Grumman about the rapidly evolving nature of missile defense, integrated battle management systems, and the technologies shaping the future of military operations.

Padorov begins by discussing how modern defense forces face a broader range of threats than ever before. Missile threats have increased in quantity, capability, and complexity, while drones and unmanned systems continue to create new operational challenges across global theaters.

A significant portion of the discussion focuses on the Integrated Battle Command System (IBCS). Developed for the U.S. Army, the system is designed to integrate information from multiple sensors and defense assets, helping commanders better understand battlefield conditions and coordinate responses to airborne threats.

The interview also explores interoperability, a critical objective for modern military operations. Padorov explains how systems like IBCS can support cooperation among allied nations while enabling greater coordination between military services and defense platforms.

Another major theme is the rise of drone warfare. Recent conflicts have demonstrated how large numbers of relatively low-cost drones can create significant operational challenges, requiring defense organizations to rethink traditional approaches to air defense and force protection.

The conversation further examines Raid Hunter, Northrop Grumman's counter-drone solution. Designed to provide a more economical means of addressing mass drone attacks and other threats, the system reflects the growing importance of cost-effective defensive capabilities in modern warfare.

The interview also highlights the balance between military effectiveness and affordability. As adversaries field increasing numbers of unmanned systems, defense organizations are seeking technologies capable of delivering reliable protection without relying exclusively on expensive interceptor systems.

Additionally, Padorov discusses future areas of innovation, including directed energy technologies, electronic warfare capabilities, cyber-enabled defense systems, and other approaches that may complement traditional air and missile defense architectures.

Another important topic is the role of integrated defense networks. By connecting sensors, shooters, command systems, and allied forces, defense organizations can improve awareness, coordination, and response times across increasingly complex operational environments.

Looking ahead, Padorov expects continued investment in air defense modernization, counter-drone systems, interoperability, and emerging technologies that can help address future battlefield requirements.

Throughout the discussion, Padorov shares perspectives on missile defense, integrated command systems, drone threats, military interoperability, electronic warfare, directed energy, defense modernization, national security, and the future of air defense operations.
